projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Virgil Roe was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: The date is September the 9th, 19 --I mean, 2004. The place of the interview is at 3915 Colby Avenue, Cascadian Place. The name of the person being interviewed is?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Virgil V. Roe.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Virgil V. Roe.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: R-o-e.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: R-o-e. I am doing the interview. My name is Adeline Eddy. I work at Cascadian Place as activity director. And we will start the interview now. The war --excuse me. What war were you in?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: World War II?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. The branch of service you were in?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I was in the field artillery.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. What was your rank?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I was a corporal. Came out as a corporal.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: In Burma, with Merrill's Marauders, and the second campaign was Mars Task Force. Both happened in northern Burma.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: That's hard to say. I quit a government job.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And picked me up 30 days __ in the end.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh, okay. Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: In Seattle.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: So you were pretty well given the choice of going in?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, I hadn't been --been given --rum --heard rumors that if you had a government job and quit, removed yourself any length of time, you were --you were headed for the Service.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Did --what service of the branch did you join?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Field artillery.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Do you recall your first days in the Service?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Somewhat. I --I was taken in - [Interview interrupted by a telephone call.]

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-oh, you want to answer that? I was taken in down in California, went to the city of Monterey, and I was fortunate the placement officer there was my high school teacher.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And he wanted to know what branch I wanted to get into. I knew I was in, there was no question about it. I chose the field artillery. He suggested --I asked for --for --well, anyway.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: How old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Twenty-three.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Did you have --did you have to go to boot camp or training?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. I went to (Cantswith), Texas, for training with the artillery, 105s.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: One of my favorite sergeants --boy, I can't think of his name now. We went through combat together. Wow.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: It might come to you a little bit later. You served in World War II?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: And that was the only war you served in? [Telephone rings.]

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: At that time that's all there was.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. And you told me you went to Burma?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: How did you like that when you arrived there?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, I was kinda numb. I was out of my realm. It was an experience.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Was it the weather, or the people, or . . .

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, the whole thing was --it's a whole new ballgame over there. We went by ships from Norfolk, Virginia, to Capetown, South Africa; Cape Town, South Africa to --oh, what's that big eastern port in India? The western --oh, I can't think of the name of that now, doggonnit. And then we took the Narrow Gage Railroad over to (Round Key?), India, and went up into Assam by Ledo, where we took off from.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Being in a different area than you've ever experienced before, did that get you closer to the --the other servicemen around you as a group? I mean, did you -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, actually there were only 3000 of us went in.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And we were up against 20 --we hiked through the Himalayas into Myitkyina. We lost troops getting there; some. We lost our leader, which was Merrill himself, and had a new leader called Colonel Hunter; very fine man. When we got to Myitkyina, we found out we were up against 20,000 Japanese __ marines. And we spent 91 days on the front line there just north of Myitkyina. We were less than a thousand yards from the enemy.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: At that time, at that time we had superiority. Thank God for little favors. And I was the --in training for the field artillery, I became the truck driver for the communications.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And they made me a telephone operator for the __ --the artillery observer, which put a lot of my time ahead of the front lines. I saw no real action to speak of. I recall being shot at a few times. I don't recall ever shooting anybody myself. Uh . . .

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations for this work?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Tell me what they are as you go.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: There's my dog tags.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh, those are wonderful.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Here's my good time medal.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Well, you're -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And here's the two stars for the two missions I was on with Merrill's Marauders-Mars Task Force. And when I was in the hospital I also got the infantry combat badge. While I was in the hospital, I spent 30 days in the hospital after Myitkyina fell, and --oh, yeah, and here's --I have a rifle sharpshooters medal.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Three Chinese officers came to the hospital and issued these medals to us. They were in the hospital. The Chinese was coming in on our right flank, we were headed north --no, headed south from the north, Burma, and the British were coming up from the south. And that's about the size of that.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: So you were injured?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I have no --no Purple Heart. Well, the last days of combat I don't recall because I was picked up and flipped into a clump of bamboo and told to stay there until it was over. My lieutenant put me in the bush and told me to stay. I wasn't able to walk. Well, started with I had injured my foot by stepping on a can --these ration can openers, mind you.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And had ingrown (feetwart).

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And that was what I was in the hospital for. The --well, they held me three --over three weeks waiting for a doctor to come in to Calcutta because the doctor they had at the field hospital didn't want to touch it because they thought I might lose my foot. Kind of a delicate situation. But I weighed 118 pounds when they drug me out. And we took a --the hospital was about three miles back behind the line, the field hospital. Can't think of the name of the darn thing. It had a number to it. Anyway, we were taken back by oxcart, drove by oxen. And we had several of the boys were walking along with us and knocking off some of the --there were two, what I recall, there were two snipers shooting at us, and the boys knocked it out going back to the hospital. Oh, while I was recuperating at the hospital, the rest of the group, which was --well, we were supposed to have been shipped home after the Merrill's Marauders combat. That didn't happen to all of us.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: A lot of us was held, and they formed a new command called Mars Task Force. And they were sent back behind the lines up the (Supaboom) Road about five miles out of Myitkyina, to a rest camp. And this rest camp was something else. It was a do-it-yourself job. But that camp was all going great by the time I got to it. And we were getting trucks in. I got back to driving trucks. And during the training there that we had - well, there was darn little training, as far as I was concerned. I was in the motor pool that they formed. We had six by sixes and some Jeeps. I had a six by six. Oh, I get to have a Jeep. I took some officers back up the (Fiddlerboom) Road about 20 miles up toward Tibet, ran into a herd of elephants.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And believe it or not, later on I learned the reason the trip was going back, I --when we drove back, the officer told me where to park, and I parked. They told me to stay; I stayed. And they went down into the I guess you call it jungle. And I waited, oh, hour, hour and a half and they came back out. But later on I heard that they --somehow they had robbed a bank and managed to stash the goodies back there. I don't know how true it was. It was just a rumor as far as I was concerned. Nice --they were a good bunch of guys.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Well, how was the food?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Nothing but (G) and K-Rations. Everything was airdropped.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Did you eat any local things around the place?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family during this time?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Very little. Very little mail going in or out.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Did you have plenty of supplies, or did you have to kind of -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well -

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Scavenger around?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I found it rather strange. Merrill's Marauders, we had nothing but --oh, what the devil? Well, we didn't have the cannons, it was __ darn, I can't think of --terrible. Old age is setting in.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Mortars. We had mortars.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Eighty-one --81-millimeter mortars, and then eventually they came up with the 120, which could do a lot of damage. Actually, what we were doing, we spent 91 days there in Myitkyina trying to knock off the Japanese, but didn't commit Hara-keri. We managed to kill, and we couldn't take --we didn't take any prisoners. There was no place to put them and no one to take care of them.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Those that we did get were interviewed and then sent back behind the lines, and . . .

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: And somebody else took care of them?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No. Well, in a sense, yes.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: They were done in. Anyway, where was I?

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Was there anything special you did to keep like a good luck charm or something you thought about that would be lucky for you, that you know -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I made a day-by-day diary, and I lost it.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And I didn't lose it until after I got home. Day by day, mind you.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh. So that was kind of what you wanted to do?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I wish I had been able to keep it.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: How did you guys entertain yourselves when you weren't worrying about everything around you?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, there was no --we were all offered leave at night.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-huh. You had a few hundred miles to go in the mountains you might get somewhere.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: It was strictly jungle. And the Japanese had the town of Myitkyina to themselves, which wasn't much of a town. Actually, Myitkyina was a --that was the stopping off place for the British noble class to go hunting.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: That was their hunting grounds. Very well known for that. And while I was in the hospital, had a black panther came through the barracks.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: That was -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: And came in underneath our bunks.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Did you play pranks on each other, anything like that?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No, no. No, there wasn't any --oh, yes, I'll take that back. Periodically some guy --somebody would get it in to decide he would holler out loud, "Here comes sergeant so-and-so who we cannot do without," any he'd draw fire. There was a little bit of that. But outside of that there's . . .

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Do you have any photographs?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No. 12

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, I have one as I got into China. See, when we got through with Merrill's Marauders, we went from Myitkyina, to Bhamo, down to Lashio. From Lashio, we had cleaned up everything and flown into China, was training Chinese officers in the art of artillery.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: So how long were you actually in the Service during the war?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I was only in 32 months.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I was in Burma somewhere between 18 and 20 months, and then I was into China about four or five months.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Do you remember the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I was --flew the long way home. From Myitkyina --I mean, from China --oh, darn, why can't I remember the name of that town? It's where the Flying Tigers were.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: It will come to you tonight.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, undoubtedly, undoubtedly. Anyway, we flew from there to Barakpur, India. From there to Abadan, Iran. From there to Triply. Now, that's the hottest spot in the world, 140 degrees. And the strangest __+. These black gentlemen were running up and down that hot airport barefooted. They must have had callouses on their feet about that thick. Oh, terrible. Anyway, from Tripoli we went to Morocco. Morocco to the Azores. From the Azores to Bermuda. From Bermuda to Florida, Miami, Florida __. And then by there I took a tube train from there to Fort Miller, where I got my discharge on ...

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Did you go into service at Fort Louis?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No, California.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: California. Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I had asked my leading man for a week off. As soon as the war started, I worked in the Navy yard. We were working ten hours a day, one day out of ten. Every tenth day we had off. Well, I was married at the time. I had children, three. And __+ women going around paying your bills and doing what you had to do. Well, the leading man, he just laughed at me. So I went to my quarterman, and he told me to get lost. So I did. The wife and I, we gave the kids to the --to her mother, and we took off and went down to California. We were only going to be gone a week. We were having too much fun. We stayed a whole month, and they __ cut up with me. Terrible. See, I'm not a hero, I'm a surviver.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Well, everyone is.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Strictly a surviver.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. The days and weeks after your service, do you remember any of them? What your feelings were? What you did?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, before leaving China, on one of the trips that I took with the hauling Chinese officers around, I had a sergeant riding in the back behind me, and I had him pounding on my back, thub, thub, thub, thub. And we had a medical officer at that time saw what was going on, and he asked me to come in and see him when we got back to camp, which I did. And then he had made arrangements --a day or two after that he informed me he had made arrangements for me to go to the hospital. And the day before I was supposed to go the hospital got washed out, which meant it would be a couple of weeks getting the hospital back into shape. I was asked a lot of questions about paralysis, and he just wanted to have me well checked over, I gather. But the point system came out. I told him what he could do with his hospital. So I came home on my points. I had 86 points. You had to have 85.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay. Now, the points consist of how much time you spent over there or what operations you were in and things like that?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. I --well, after we got back --after I got back, the Rangers took us in.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Now, I didn't have --I did not go through any Ranger training. It was all on-the-job training. 15

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, brother. Anyway --oh, the doctor informed me when I told him I wasn't going to no hospital, he said when you get discharged, declare everything from the bottom of your feet to the top of your head. So I did.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, I had --I had jungle rot, and going through some of the rice paddies I had leeches up to my knees all over me, and I went through a lot of crap. Anyway, it was --it was no picnic.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, then I had malaria came back on me. Oh, that's - that's --I went to hospital twice. Once right after the __ combat __+ Mars Task Force, we were marching south down towards Bhamo, and every day there in Burma we were given Atabrine tablets. You know what Atabrine tablets are for?

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Malaria?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: An officer --we all line up. There would be an officer handing out an Atabrine tablet, another --a non-commissioned officer was handing you a little cup of water to take it. Well, for three days in a row I did that all right, but I didn't take more than three or four steps after I drank the water and I'd throw up. I had what they called gastritis. Well, I got to the place where I couldn't even walk. I rode a horse for three days. There was a little experience there that I certainly do remember. See, we had no doctors on the --on the trail at all. We had a veterinarian. And he did me a couple of favors. Anyway, he got me this --put me on this horse, and every hour, ten minutes out of every hour there'd be a break, marching break. By the way, I was --I was hauling a mule around. That mule --I was not hauling the mule, believe me. That mule was carrying a breach, block and two wheels to the - oh, we had the old French 75 cannons, if you can believe that. See, the United States very gracefully gave all the artillery, actual artillery, the 105s, to the Chinese to use. I never did get that one figured out. Anyway, on this one occasion when we stopped for our break, I got off the horse and was laying down, had a long halter shank rope on the rope --on the horse, and he was quite a distance from me and we had a clunking sound, and then everybody scattered. And I was told to go see what that horse was messing around with. And a 250-pound bomb dud, and that horse __ --well, we got out of there in a hurry, believe me. Anyway, that's one of those little experiences that we could (?avoid it?).

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: After you were out, did you continue your friendships with people that you had been in with?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No, I didn't. I didn't get too friendly with any - with anybody. Didn't feel like --things just didn't feel right for me.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Did you have --have you ever joined any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Oh, yeah, VFW.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: VFW?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Uh-huh. I transferred down to Arizona when I retired, and then from there I transferred up here to Everett.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: What did you do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I worked for my father in the theater business. Dad had five theaters in Seattle, all neighborhood theaters. I had the Broadway.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Did the military experience influence your thinking about war and about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, it's a necessary evil, I'll promise you that. I'm mighty thankful we're not letting them come over here to do their dirty work.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: As much as they have done, it's too bad. We're not out of it yet. 18

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: No. What kinds of activities do your --did you do with like the VFW? [Telephone rings.]

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Just general club things?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I didn't go to the meetings very much.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: However, I went to some of their dances.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Do --did you ever have any reunions with your troop?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I did with --I went to one reunion with Merrill's Marauders and one with Mars Task Force. The one with Mars Task Force, it was back in Ohio, Columbus, Ohio, back in 1960 --1992. And then I went to a Merrill's -

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Marauders?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: --Marauders deal in Phoenix, which was quite small. And now they're having all the get-togethers down at the --at Laughlin.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: At the Riverside Hotel.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Are you planning on going there?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: No, no, I never did.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Did --did the service experiences affect your life or change you in any way that you can -

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, getting out, I got out total disability.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh. 19

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Which has made my life almost too good.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: I didn't --didn't take out any insurance. The VA was taking care of all my medical __+. They passed me up the last two days. DAV just --I had two --oh, month before last they were supposed to pick me up and take me to the VA, and then today they were supposed to take me to the VA. They didn't show up.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: I want to thank you for this interview.

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: Well, didn't --sure didn't amount to much, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Well, I think it's very interesting. And could I have your permission to take pictures of your medals and a picture of you to send in?

sp.speaker: Virgil Roe
sp.p: If you insist.

sp.speaker: Adeline Eddy
sp.p: Oh, thank you. And you can even smile. Thank you so much. Virgil Roe. [Interview concluded.]
